content:
<think>
Mode is greenfield, so I am producing a fresh ProductRoadmap from the problem statement rather than amending an existing one.

The problem: the real Slack ingress for jarvis is the `jarvis serve-nats` systemd user unit, but the repo only versions the wrong unit (`jarvis-frontdoor.service`, which runs langgraph dev). Two consequences follow: (a) the box cannot be rebuilt from the repo — the actual door is unversioned; (b) nothing detects when serve-nats's NATS subscription goes stale, which is an absent-operator failure with no self-recovery — the door goes silently quiet.

The statement pre-decomposes into three deliverables, and they map cleanly onto three features under a single epic:

1. Version the real `jarvis-serve-nats.service` into `ops/systemd/`, with a coordinator install step matching the existing `jarvis-frontdoor` README pattern. This must come first: the watchdog needs a canonical, versioned unit name to journal-read, and the install pattern already exists to copy.
2. A watchdog that reads `journalctl --user -u jarvis-serve-nats` for socket/subscription staleness and alerts Slack when the door goes quiet. Key design hazard: the thing being watched IS the Slack door — the alert path must not route through serve-nats itself, or a dead door silences its own alarm. The alert must leave via an out-of-band path (direct Slack webhook/API call from the watchdog script). The watchdog also needs a staleness definition (no subscription-activity/heartbeat lines within a threshold window) and must avoid alert-storming (cooldown/deduplication).
3. Correct the O-30 register row so it names serve-nats — not langgraph dev — as the Slack door. Small, independent, but it is the record of truth being wrong today, so it ships in the same epic.

Scope fences from the statement, honored as explicit constraints: ops files + a watchdog script only; no app source changes; no compose deploy (this is a systemd-user-unit world); jarvis is not a DCL venue, so no DCL capture/corpus work rides along.

Sequencing: FT-01 → FT-02 (watchdog depends on the versioned unit name and install pattern); FT-03 is independent and can land any time. Priorities: the watchdog is the mission (P0), the unit versioning is its prerequisite (P0), the register correction is P1.

Risks worth naming: journalctl text parsing is brittle across log-format drift; a quiet channel is ambiguous (no traffic vs. dead subscription) — the staleness signal must key on the subscription/socket lifecycle lines, not mere message absence, or accept a heartbeat-style probe; timer-based scheduling (systemd user timer) keeps the watchdog itself supervised rather than a daemon nobody watches.
</think>
